display_title: Official Review of Paper1205 by Reviewer nHMn

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This submission presents an omni-supervised representation learning with a hierarchical strategy that takes both fully-supervised and self-supervised contrastive learning into account. The experiments have been done on ImageNet-1k for the pre-training and have been evaluated on a bunch of datasets for downstream tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
	- The idea of omni-supervised to get the benefits of both available labeled and unlabeled data is interesting.
	- There has been an effort in running different sets of experiments on different downstream tasks and for ablation studies to show the effect of different components in this pipeline.

Weaknesses:

1-  While I like the idea of omni-supervised representation learning, the way this problem has been stated in this submission only considers a single curated dataset, ImageNet-1k.  Getting benefits from both labeled and unlabeled data makes more sense when we consider different sources of data such as one large uncurated data without labels and one curated dataset such as ImageNet-1k with labels. There is another work in the literature from ECCV2020 which has not been mentioned in this paper named:  "Omni-sourced Webly-supervised Learning for Video Recognition, ECCV 2020" and the idea is how to get the benefit of some sources of data that are available through the web and combine it with other sources of data with labels. While I understand that the authors try to show combining fully-supervised and self-supervised learning would bring more to the accuracy of down-stream tasks compared to only fully-supervised or self-supervised learning, I still believe that this approach is not able to be applicable in scenarios where we only have access to unlabeled data. This approach needs access to labeled data and can only improve the fully-supervised representation learning and not the self-supervised ones. To sum it up, this approach is basically introducing a fully-supervised approach where an additional loss is also utilized without any labels. 

2- I think for this approach equations and propositions have been overutilized and this brings more ambiguity to the text. 

3- There are a number of recent self-supervised representation learning in the literature that considers the task of "masking and predicting" and they are very successful in representation learning such as: Masked Autoencoders Are Scalable Vision Learners, CVPR 2022. I can suggest authors think about how they can advance these approaches in the future with the idea of omni-supervised learning considering getting benefits from different sources of labeled and unlabeled data.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The method is simple, easy to follow and seems easy to reproduce but the idea is not novel enough.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This approach basically introduces a fully-supervised approach where an additional loss based on self-supervised contrastive learning has been utilized. In my opinion, this approach is not completely an Omni-supervised learning approach where different sources of data with and without labels can be used to improve the accuracy of downstream tasks. Here is the definition of Omni-supervised learning from "Data Distillation: Towards Omni-Supervised Learning" :
"Omni-supervised learning is a special regime of semi-supervised learning in which the learner exploits all available labeled data plus internet-scale sources of unlabeled data."

To sum up, this idea is not novel enough and needs further investigations and experiments to be a valuable paper for the community, especially the experiments that demonstrate the effect of "additional" unlabeled data.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a new pretraining method, OPERA, which combines supervised and self-supervised learning in a unified formulation. Particularly, it proposes to resolve the contradiction between the contrastive self-supervised loss and the supervised signal by an extra MLP head for the supervised branch. The paper provides evaluations on the ImageNet1k recognition and downstream tasks, e.g. CIFAR classification, ADE20K segmentation, etc.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

**[S1]** Topic: the paper studies if self-supervised *(SSL) + supervised (SL) learning* > *SSL-only* or *SL-only*. I believe it is an open question that is worthy to explore. It is also related to the research about comparing the transferability of SSL and SL pretraining. It would be interesting to understand if SSL and SL are complementary. 

**[S2]** Experiment: evaluations and ablations with different settings for different tasks are provided.

**[S3]** Presentation: the writing is clear.

---

Weaknesses

**[W1]** Evaluation. At this moment, I’m not sure if the experiments justify that *SSL+SL* > *SL-only*, this is my main concern

i) Table 1 and 2, imagenet1k evaluation.

As OPERA learns with the ground-truth labels in both the pretraining (SSL+SL, 300 epochs) and the finetuning (SL, 90-200 epochs) stages, the comparison between OPERA and the *SL-only* baseline in Table 1 and 2 looks misleading, e.g. OPERA is trained with the ground-truth labels for at least 390 epochs while SL-only is trained for at most 300 epochs.

* For DeiT-S, I believe it is more reasonable to compare the last line in Table 1 and the first line in Table 2: OPERA (390 epochs) vs SL (300 epochs): 73.7 vs 79.8. Here the linear classification and finetuning protocols are comparable as OPERA is pretrained with the ground-truth labels. This comparison shows that OPERA performs worse (-6.1%) than *SL-only*.

* For R50 (table 1), it would be better to also include the *SL-only* baseline in table 1. From the [pytorch benchmark](https://pytorch.org/vision/main/models/generated/torchvision.models.resnet50.html), *SL-only* achieves a top-1 accuracy of 76.1% in 90 epochs, outperforming OPERA (390 epochs, 74.8%) by 1.3%.

Overall, the results seem to suggest that, combining SSL and SL performs worse than *SL-only* on ImageNet1k.

ii) Table 3 and 4, evaluation of downstream tasks

* R50 results in Table 3. The performance of the *SL-only* baseline in Table 3 is worse than what was presented in the [SimCLR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05709) paper. SimCLR reports top-1 accuracies of 98.3, 88.7, 98.0, 93.2 for the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Flowers-102, and Pets benchmarks, which are +0.1, +1.9, +2.4, +0.5 better than OPERA. I understand that the *SL-only* baseline in Table 3 is a re-implementation. It would be better that the authors could clarify the difference between this re-implementation and the SimCLR evaluation.

* DeiT-S results in Table 3. The performance gaps between OPERA and SL-only are marginal for CIFAR-10 (0.2%), Flowers-102 (0.1%), Pets(0.3%).

* ADE20K results in Table 4. Not sure why the results of OPERA-PT300-DeiT-B-BatchSize1024 are in bold as they are worse than the *SL-only* baseline.

At this moment, the claim that OPERA > *SL-only* for downstream tasks is not convincing.

**[W2]** Interpretation. Compared to *SL-only*, OPERA has two extra components: a) SSL loss; b) MLP head for the SL branch. To better understand the benefit of individual components, it would be better to also include the baseline: *SL-only-with-MLP-head*. It is shown in the paper [Revisiting the transferability of supervised pretraining: an mlp perspective (CVPR 2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.00496) that *SL-only-with-MLP-head* > *SL-only*. I believe comparing OPERA to *SL-only-with-MLP-head* is necessary in order to show that the improvement of OPERA is not solely from the MLP-head. 

Ablations along the chain: *SL-only* → *SL-only-with-MLP-head* → *SL-only-with-MLP-head + SSL* (OPERA) could potentially provide more information to help interpret the results of OPERA. 

**[W3]** The contradiction in Eq. (5) only appears in contrastive-based SSL methods. It is not clear if the OPERA-like method could be beneficial to other SSL methods, e.g. SwAV, DINO, etc.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: In general, the paper is written clearly. The proposed method is new to me. I believe it could be reproduced. The authors are suggested to include extra clarifications on the re-implementation in Table 3 and 4, as discussed in [W1].
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a new pretraining method, OPERA, which combines both SSL and SL signals. The research could potentially help reveal if SSL is complementary to SL for pretraining, other than as an extra regularization. However, at this moment, I don’t think the claims in the paper. e.g. OPERA > *SL-only*, etc, are well supported by the experiments, as discussed in the weaknesses section.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper explores whether combining self-supervised learning and fully supervised learning can further improves the transferability. The authors first find that a simple combination results in contradictory training signals and propose omni-supervised representation learning with hierarchical supervision (OPERA). Rather than combining the self-supervised and fully-supervised learning signals directly, the authors propose to adaptively balance two weights upon two training signals, where the two weights modulate the contributions of two signals. Furthermore, the authors introduce hierarchical representation space, with the self-supervised representation as lower-level representation, and the full-supervised representation as higher-level representation. 

The authors conduct experiments on ImageNet and compare to multiple existing self-supervised methods and the supervised baseline to show that the proposed OPERA method performs better than self-supervised pre-training in several downstream tasks: image classification, object detection and instance segmentation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ The proposed method is simple and seems to provide an effective solution for combining self-supervised and full-supervised learning.

+ The authors conduct quite same experiments to evaluate the proposed approach when changing different factors of the methods such as datasets, backbones, downstream datasets, and downstream tasks. 

- An important baseline of combining self-supervised and full-supervised learning by (1) first performing self-supervised learning, and (2) then perform self-supervised learning and full-supervised learning jointly without hierarchical representation space is missing. 

- The terminology of "omni-supervised learning" misaligns with existing literature [a] that uses "omni-supervised" to denote the settings of weakly-supervised, semi-supervised learning. Please explain about what omni-supervised learning means in general, and how does the studied setting differs from existing works. 

- The paper does not include the comparison to an important existing method (UDA) [b] which also combines supervised and unsupervised/self-supervised learning into one learning framework. UDA does not introduce hierarchical representation space, but still performs well. As the main contribution of this paper is to introduce the two-level hierarchical representation, it would be necessary to compare with the existing work UDA that does not use such hierarchical representation. 

- Some visual illustration needs improvement. For instance, the texts in Figure 5, 6, 7, 8 are too small to read. 

[a] UFO2: A Unified Framework towards Omni-supervised Object Detection. ECCV2020
[b] Unsupervised Data Augmentation for Consistency Training. NeuRIPS2020
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
The proposed method is easy to follow and implement. The paper is clearly written, although some parts (visual illustration of Figure 5-9) can be further improved with better clarity. 

Quality: 
The authors provide some good insight about why self-supervised and full-supervised learning signals may be contradictory and propose a solution to combine self-supervised and full-supervised learning signals more effectively. However, there are some concerns regarding (1) missing comparison to important baseline, and the existing method UDA [b], as well as (2) ambiguities of terminology "omni-supervised" in comparison to the existing work [a] that use it in different context.  

Novelty: 
Combining self-supervised and full-supervised learning is a simple and intuitive idea, and similar learning framework has already been studied and explored in [b]. Although the authors identify a different issue of this learning framework beyond the existing work, it is unclear of the proposed method is truly effective without experiments and further discussion to justify its novelty. 

Reproducibility:
The authors provide code in the supplementary, so there is no reproducibility issue.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents a simple and seems to provide an effective solution for self-supervised and full-supervised learning. However, there are missing important comparison of relevant baseline and related method, which makes the contributions of this paper unclear. Further, terminology of the proposed learning framework seems to be contradictory of other existing work. It is suggested to add the missing comparison with additional experiments and discussion, and change the terminology.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a hierarchical representation to learn from both supervised and contrastive loss. The observation is that the instance-level labelling could be seen a finer-grained refinement of the class-level representation. This is embedded into the architecture by having subsequent linear projection layers and applying the losses at different points of the projections so the model can capture the finer grained associated to instance discrimination first, and then cluster together into classes at the end of the second projection.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
The method relies on some credible intuition on the hierarchical nature of our approach. The technical approach is well aligned with the intuition.
The results show gains over MoCoV3, both on ImageNet linear probe as well as on downstream tasks. The first one is obvious given the nature of the learning but the second one can be considered a positive result.
The problem tackled is an important one and obtaining gains is not easy at all.

Weaknesses:
The methodology is explained in an overcomplicated manner (see below for the "clarity" comment)
Baselines: it would be nice to compare against methods that also make use of the imagenet labels. The obvious omission is the supervised contrastive learning. Other baselines can be self-referential, as in some alternative ways of combining both. Right now experiments show that if you take labels into account, it can work better, which is somewhat unsurprising.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The methodology is laid out in a way that is not so easy to follow. This should not be the case as it is a simple method with a simple formulation. There is an effort to unify the formulation for instance and class discrimination through abstracting out some of the elements. This creates confusion rather than clarity. The method does not really rely on such unification. Overall, the authors could be more careful at introducing the nomenclature in advance of the formulas - for example, Eq. 1 involves a lot of notation that has not been introduced, and the next paragraph or two goes about explaining what everything is. Maybe this should be the other way round? Eq. 8 might be a bit wrong - aren't the Y involved the spaces rather than the instances? A simplified nomenclature would make it easier for the authors to keep consistency and for the reader to follow better.
Just as a suggestion (not sure if it would work out): would it be easier to make Table 2 a figure?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper starts with an interesting idea, but it needs a bit more conclusive evidence that what they are arguing and proposing is the right methodology and some further comparisons should be included.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
